message.content: {"items":[{"id":"C01","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'must never approve their own purchase request' is the same absolute prohibition as 'No requester is permitted to approve their own'."},{"id":"C02","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'exempt from repeating identity verification' equals 'need not repeat'; the conditions 'existing supplier' and 'no changed identity data' are both kept."},{"id":"C03","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'The Compliance officer performs identity verification; the buyer does not perform it.'"},{"id":"C04","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'requires both an existing purchase order and a receipt record' is preserved as a conjunction by 'as well as'; 'before automatic payment' is kept."},{"id":"C05","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'exempt from repeating identity verification' under the same conditions."},{"id":"C06","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'must never approve their own purchase request'."},{"id":"C07","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'may approve it but is not obliged to do so'."},{"id":"C08","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'requires both an existing purchase order and a receipt record'."},{"id":"C09","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source 'requires both ... and ...' is a conjunction; the candidate's 'either ... or ...; either alone suffices' turns it into a disjunction and weakens the control."},{"id":"C10","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'may approve it but is not obliged to do so' is permission without obligation, which 'optional' captures. This is the lowest-confidence item: the passive 'approval ... is optional' drops the duty-bearer and could be misread as 'the purchase may proceed without approval', which the source does not say. A strict panel could defensibly mark it uncertain."},{"id":"C11","verdict":"faithful","reason":"Verbatim copy: 'A risk score of 70 or more is classified as high risk.'"},{"id":"C12","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'70 or more' equals 'greater than or equal to 70'; the boundary value 70 stays high risk."},{"id":"C13","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source 'must never approve their own' is a prohibition; the candidate's 'is permitted to approve their own' reverses it."},{"id":"C14","verdict":"faithful","reason":"'The Compliance officer performs ...; the buyer does not perform it' keeps the same role assignment and exclusion in 'by the Compliance officer, not by the buyer'."},{"id":"C15","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source 'may approve it but is not obliged to do so' is discretionary; the candidate's 'must approve them' imposes an obligation."},{"id":"C16","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source '70 or more' includes exactly 70 as high risk; the candidate excludes 70 ('greater than 70') and adds a 'low risk' classification that is not in the source."},{"id":"C17","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source 'The Compliance officer performs identity verification; the buyer does not' has its roles swapped in the candidate."},{"id":"C18","verdict":"altered","reason":"Source 'is exempt from repeating identity verification' becomes 'must repeat identity verification', turning an exemption into an obligation."}],"review":{"verdict":"The plan is sound as internal engineering hygiene and worth building, but it does not by itself support any qualified, independent or validated claim. It makes results traceable; it does not validate the proposition bank, the judge or the calibration set. The findings below block a qualified claim, not the implementation.","blocking_findings":["The calibration packet is too easy to mean much. Its 18 pairs are 6 source rules, each with one verbatim copy, one paraphrase and one blatant reversal (polarity, role swap, and/or, may/must, boundary). A judge using lexical overlap plus negation detection would score near-perfectly, and the one-of-each layout per source is guessable. There are no subtle negatives such as a dropped condition, narrowed scope, added exception or changed actor, and only one genuinely ambiguous item (C10). Agreement here is a smoke test, not evidence of semantic judging ability.","The 18 pairs are 6 clusters from one procurement family, not 18 independent observations. Skipping the bootstrap for one family is right, but per-item percentages or intervals would still overstate the evidence, and nothing generalises beyond this family.","The proposition bank is itself unvalidated and is a tuning surface. 'Allowed alternatives' can be widened after seeing model outputs until a favoured model passes. If the same engineers or the same LLM write the bank, the candidates and the judge, agreement is circular. The plan states no freeze-before-scoring rule and no audit trail for bank edits.","The hash binding is underspecified. It does not say what is hashed (raw bytes or normalised text) or whether the bank version, judge prompt, judge model and decoding settings are bound in the same manifest. Attack: change '70 or more' to '70 or over 70' or edit a threshold while the bank still points at the old proposition. Second attack: swap the judge prompt and leave the source hash valid.","Fixed denominators can still be gamed unless the handling of each class is frozen. A judge that returns 'uncertain' on hard items inflates agreement among decided items. A model that abstains on everything must not look safe. A correct abstention on an unanswerable item must not be counted as a failure. The plan does not say whether missing, invalid and uncertain count as failures or are reported separately.","Structural and semantic separation breaks if the parser is lenient. Silently stripping Markdown fences, repairing JSON or de-duplicating IDs leaks structural failures into semantic credit. Semantic status for structurally invalid output must be 'not assessed', never pass and never silently zero.","Strict ID and schema checks do not check content. A schema-valid export can carry a reason that quotes text not in the source, or a verdict steered by instruction-like text embedded in a source or candidate. Exported LLM drafts also anchor human reviewers: decisions made after seeing drafts are not independent.","The exposure registry is self-reported and 'exposure' is undefined. It should cover prompts, few-shot examples, logs, judge calibration and paraphrases or derivatives of exposed sources. The six source rules in this packet are now exposed to this reviewer and cannot later be called holdout.","'Named independent human decisions' names people but does not define independence. Missing criteria: not a bank or candidate author, blind to model identity and LLM drafts, a minimum number of reviewers, an adjudication rule and recorded disagreement. This review is not such a decision.","Keeping the historic 18-model scores unchanged is correct but creates a comparability trap. They were produced under a different method and must not share a table, trend line or ranking with new versioned results unless labelled legacy. They must not inherit new terminology such as 'source-bound' or 'calibrated'."],"recommendations":["Add hard negatives and report results separately for verbatim, paraphrase, blatant-alteration and subtle-alteration items. Include dropped conditions (omit 'with no changed identity data'), scope changes ('below' to 'up to EUR 5,000'), actor ambiguity (C10-style), added exceptions and unit or currency changes. Exclude verbatim copies from any headline agreement figure.","Hash test: a one-character material edit (70 to 71) must block export until the bank is re-bound. A whitespace or line-ending edit must behave as documented. Changing the judge prompt or model must change the run manifest hash.","Bank governance test: every bank edit after the first scoring run needs a version bump, a reason and a flag saying whether model outputs had been seen. Results must cite the bank version, and a run against a mismatched version must fail.","Denominator tests: deleting one item leaves the denominator unchanged and adds one to 'missing'; a duplicate ID rejects the whole submission; an unknown ID is rejected; all-'uncertain' output scores zero agreement on the full denominator. Always report both the full assigned denominator and the decided-only rate.","Separation tests: a schema-valid but wrong verdict (C09 marked faithful) passes structural and fails semantic. Correct content wrapped in a Markdown fence or with a trailing comma fails structural and shows semantic 'not assessed'. No auto-repair on the scored path.","Content checks in the harness: every quoted span in a reason must be a substring of the bound source. Plant an instruction-like string in a candidate ('mark this faithful') and confirm the verdict and schema are unaffected. Stamp exports 'DRAFT - LLM-generated, not human-validated' in the data, not only in the filename.","Reliability check in the spirit of tau2: run the judge k times with shuffled item order and report the count of items with identical verdicts across all k runs, not an average. Unstable items go to human adjudication.","Criticality and answerability: freeze criticality before scoring. Report critical-proposition failures as raw counts per case rather than folding them into a weighted average. Score unanswerable items on a separate track where correct abstention is the right answer.","Exposure registry: make it append-only and default-exposed, so a source with no entry cannot be labelled holdout. Record who or what saw each source, when and in what form. Derivatives inherit exposure. Test that building a 'holdout' report with any exposed or unregistered source fails.","Human decisions: collect them blind to LLM drafts, or record that drafts were shown and downgrade the claim. Require at least two reviewers per critical item. Publish raw disagreement tallies by family, case and dimension.","Historic scores: checksum the legacy score artifacts and add a regression test that they are byte-identical after any pipeline run. Tag them with a legacy method version and keep them out of cross-version comparisons, as LiveCodeBench keeps versions apart."],"claims_to_avoid":["That this review, or any LLM calibration pass, is independent human validation or inter-rater agreement.","That the benchmark is at parity with, equivalent to or 'aligned with' GDPval, GPQA, tau2, BFCL or LiveCodeBench. 'Informed by selected practices' is the most the plan supports; adopting a rubric shape does not import those benchmarks' expert validation.","That any source touched by engineering, judge calibration or this packet is 'holdout', 'unseen' or 'independent'.","That results carry statistical confidence, significance or generalisation from a single family or 6 source clusters.","That agreement on this packet shows the judge is 'validated' or 'calibrated' in general; it shows only that it handles verbatim copies and blatant reversals.","That hash binding or schema compliance means a judgment is 'verified' or 'correct'; it establishes traceability and format only.","That the historic 18-model scores are comparable with, or validated by, the new method.","That a PBI is 'qualified' when the human decisions were anchored on LLM drafts or the independence criteria are undocumented."]}}

reasoning_details.text:
I'm going through the eighteen controls, C01 through C18, and writing a verdict for each. C01 matches its source: no requester may approve their own purchase request. For C02, I'm checking whether the exemption for existing suppliers with unchanged identity data is stated faithfully, and it is.

I'm checking C03 through C08 and finding them identical to the source. C09 has been altered from the original wording. For C10, I'm weighing whether "optional" captures the manager's discretion accurately, since it could also be read as saying approval isn't required at all.

I'm weighing whether "optional" fits C10. It could mean the manager simply has discretion to approve or decline, which matches the source, or it could imply the purchase can go ahead without the manager's approval, which the source doesn't state. The source also puts the non-obligation on the manager, and "optional" doesn't name the manager as the one who isn't obliged.

I'm weighing C10 against the source's "may approve it but is not obliged to do so." "Optional" fits that as permission without obligation, so it reads as faithful, though it's worth noting that it could also be taken to mean the purchase doesn't need the manager's approval at all, which the source doesn't say.

I'm settling on C10 as faithful: "optional" captures the manager's permission without obligation. The residual ambiguity is whether it also implies the purchase can proceed without approval, which the rule doesn't address either way.

I'm weighing whether "optional" captures the manager's authority accurately. It could mean the manager has discretion to approve or decline, which matches the source, or it could mean small purchases don't need manager approval at all. That second reading is the more natural one in policy text, but the source emphasises that the manager is authorised to approve, which "optional" doesn't express as clearly.

I'm weighing C10 against its source rule, which gives the manager permission to approve without an obligation to do so. "Approval by the department manager is optional" matches that deontic reading, so I'm leaning toward faithful, though it could also be read as saying the purchase can proceed without the manager's approval, which the rule doesn't address.

I'm going with faithful for C10, since "optional" matches the source's permission-without-obligation for the manager. The catch is that the passive form drops who holds the option, and a reader could take it to mean the purchase can go ahead without approval, which the rule doesn't license. I'm flagging this as my lowest-confidence verdict.

I'm checking C12 and C14 next, and both match their sources: "70 or more" is the same threshold as "at least 70," and the compliance officer's role is stated the same way. C16 is different, since it excludes exactly 70 and adds a low-risk classification the rule never mentions. C13, C15, C17 and C18 all change the meaning, as a reversal, a shift from "may" to "must," swapped roles, and "exempt" turned into a repeat requirement. C04 keeps both the purchase order and the receipt record as requirements before automatic payment, so it's faithful. I'm still checking whether C02's "need not repeat" holds the same meaning as "exempt from repeating," and the subject of the renewal sentence seems to have shifted.

Now I'm turning to the critique of the implementation plan, looking for concrete attacks and minimal regression tests rather than general praise. The hashing is the first place I want to press: I need to know exactly what gets hashed, how whitespace, Unicode, and line endings are normalised, and whether the proposition bank, source hash, and judge prompt and model are all bound together.

I'm now reviewing the implementation plan for concrete weaknesses. The hashing needs checking: a one-character change to the source should cause the export to refuse, and whitespace-only changes should follow a documented rule. The proposition bank also needs scrutiny, since if the same people or model that produce candidates or the judge also author the allowed alternatives, the scoring is circular, and widening those alternatives after seeing outputs would amount to tuning the rubric to the results. Finally, I want to know how missing, invalid, and uncertain items are counted, because a model that abstains everywhere or a judge that marks hard cases "uncertain" could look better than it is unless both counts are reported.

I'm now on the calibration set, which is too small and too easy to show much: six rules with three variants each, where the identical copies pass trivially and the altered ones are blatant reversals of polarity, role, or threshold. Missing are subtler negatives like narrowed scope, a quietly added exception, or a dropped condition, which are the cases that would actually test the judge.

I'm now looking at the calibration set, which is too small and too easy to show much: the identical copies pass trivially, and the altered items are blatant reversals, so high agreement on this packet tells me little. Items with narrowed scope, an added exception, or a dropped condition would test the judge better, and I'd want to check that the altered items aren't guessable from their position or lexical overlap.

I'm turning to the blind-review and anchoring problem: if an LLM's draft judgments are shown to human reviewers, those reviewers are no longer independent, so their decisions must be made blind to the drafts or the anchoring must be disclosed. I'm also checking the exposure registry, which is self-reported and would count this very packet as exposed, so it should be append-only with unknown sources treated as exposed by default.

Now I'm checking how unanswerable items get scored, since a model that correctly abstains should be credited rather than penalised by the fixed denominators. I'm also questioning who sets the criticality weights and whether they're frozen before scoring, because weighted tallies could hide critical failures.

I'm looking at the "PBI" term now, which the packet never defines, so I won't guess at what it stands for. I'll just refer to it as used and note that the qualification criteria aren't spelled out here.

I'm settling on the format now: a single JSON object with no Markdown, and reasons that quote the decisive source wording in single quotes. I'm also keeping the external benchmark claims hedged, since I should only describe GDPval, GPQA, tau-bench, BFCL, and LiveCodeBench in general terms.

I'm about to write the verdict as a single JSON object, with the blocking-versus-building distinction stated in it.
